summary: This standards-track specification lists standard mailbox names for reaching common roles at an organization, so you know where to send a message even without knowing who works there.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 2142 lists the email addresses that any organisation with internet services should accept. Names such as postmaster, abuse and hostmaster point at roles rather than people, so a stranger can reach the right desk without knowing who works there.

The document also fixes the rules those names have to obey: they must work at the top level of the organisation's domain, they must not depend on capitalisation, and a mail server that handles mail for a domain has to accept them even when that server does not run the service itself.

questions: what is the postmaster email address
subtitle: The standard set of email addresses for reaching an organisation's people and services.

tldr.problem: Several protocols already expected a fixed mailbox name at every site, such as POSTMASTER for mail and USENET for news, and other names had become custom practice. No single document collected them, so an organisation had to guess which addresses outsiders might try.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2142 lists the mailbox names an organisation should support, grouped by business role, network operation and internet service. It states the scope rules: a name must work at the top level of the organisation's domain, regardless of character case, and mail exchangers must accept it for a domain even when they do not run the service themselves.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Standards Track specification from May 1997 with no successor. It also warns that a widely known set of addresses makes it easier to flood a mailbox with junk.

facts.label: Case handling
facts.value: Mailbox names are recognised regardless of character case

facts.label: Mailing list rule
facts.value: LIST-REQUEST@DOMAIN is required for a list at LIST@DOMAIN

facts.label: DNS recommendation
facts.value: HOSTMASTER@domain, a simple word without metacharacters

facts.label: Autonomous system example
facts.value: AS3557@RA.NET reaches the technical contact for Autonomous System 3557

today: RFC 2142 is a Standards Track specification published in May 1997. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so the names it lists are still the ones the document defines. Its one warning stands on its own: the wider these addresses become known, the easier they are to flood.

sections.title: Rationale and Scope
sections.content:
Several internet documents had already fixed mailbox names for the operators of a new service. RFC 822 requires a POSTMASTER@domain mailbox on every host that has an SMTP server. Other protocols had de facto standards, such as USENET@domain for NNTP and WEBMASTER@domain for HTTP. Names that belong to no particular protocol also had a custom standard, such as ABUSE@domain and TROUBLE@domain.

The purpose of the document is to gather and specify the basic set of mailbox names that organisations need to support. Most organisations do not need the whole set, because not every organisation offers every service. But if a service is offered, the mailbox name associated with it must be supported, so that delivery reaches a recipient appropriate for that service or role.

A host that does not accept mail directly but does implement a service covered by this document must have an MX RR set, and the mail exchangers named by that set must treat the referenced host's domain name as local for the purpose of accepting mail for the defined mailbox name. This holds even when the advertised domain name differs from the host's own domain name: an NNTP server whose host name is DATA.RAMONA.VIX.COM but which advertises VIX.COM in its Path headers must have mail deliverable both to USENET@VIX.COM and to USENET@DATA.RAMONA.VIX.COM, even if the two reach different final destinations.

The scope of a well known mailbox name is its domain name. Servers that accept mail on behalf of a domain must accept and correctly process mailbox names for that domain, even when the server itself does not support the associated service. An NNTP server that advertises the organisation's top level domain in its Path headers therefore obliges the mail exchangers for that top level domain to accept mail to USENET@domain, even when those exchangers do not themselves serve NNTP.
sections.plainLanguage:
The document exists because a fixed set of addresses had already spread informally across the internet, one per service and one per job. Putting them in one specification means a stranger can try postmaster@example.com and reach a person who can act.

It also draws a line around responsibility. The mail server that handles mail for a domain is the one that has to accept the address, even if the service behind the address runs on a different machine.

sections.title: Invariants
sections.content:
For well known names that are not tied to a specific protocol, only the organisation's top level domain name has to be valid. If an internet service provider's domain name is COMPANY.COM, then ABUSE@COMPANY.COM must be valid and supported, even though the customers whose activity generates the complaints use hosts with more specific names such as SHELL1.COMPANY.COM. It is valid and encouraged to support mailbox names for sub-domains as well, where appropriate.

Mailbox names must be recognised independently of character case. POSTMASTER, postmaster, Postmaster, PostMaster and even PoStMaStEr are the same name, and delivery goes to the same mailbox.

Implementations of these well known names have to take account of what the senders who use them expect. Sending back an automatic mail acknowledgement is usually helpful, though the document suggests caution about the possibility of duelling mail robots and the resulting mail loops.
sections.plainLanguage: Three rules hold everywhere. The name has to work at the top level of the domain, it must not matter how the letters are capitalised, and a reply to it should normally come automatically so the sender knows it arrived.

sections.title: The Mailbox Name Catalogue
sections.content:
The names for line-of-business activities are grouped first. INFO carries packaged information about the organisation, its products or its services, and is often tied to an autoresponder with a range of standard files available. MARKETING handles product marketing and marketing communications, SALES handles product purchase information, and SUPPORT handles problems with a product or service.

The network operations names provide recourse for customers, providers and others who are having difficulty with the organisation's internet service. ABUSE, in customer relations, deals with inappropriate public behaviour. NOC, in network operations, deals with the network infrastructure. SECURITY, in network security, deals with security bulletins or queries.

Each major internet protocol service has a mailbox for receiving queries and reports. POSTMASTER belongs to SMTP, HOSTMASTER to DNS, USENET to NNTP, WEBMASTER to HTTP, UUCP to UUCP and FTP to FTP. Two synonyms are kept because of their extensive installed base: NEWS is a synonym for USENET, and WWW is a synonym for WEBMASTER.
sections.plainLanguage: The catalogue has three groups. Names for business roles, names for network operations, and one name per internet service. The service names are the ones outsiders are most likely to try, and two older spellings are kept as synonyms because so many sites already use them.

sections.title: Mailing List Administration
sections.content:
Mailing lists have an administrative mailbox name where add and drop requests and other meta-queries can be sent. For a mailing list whose submission mailbox name is LIST@DOMAIN, there must be an administrative mailbox name LIST-REQUEST@DOMAIN.

Distribution list management software such as MajorDomo and Listserv also has a single mailbox name associated with the software on that system, usually the name of the software rather than the name of a particular list. Using such a mailbox name requires participants to know what list software the site runs, which the document calls problematic. It therefore states that list-specific -REQUEST mailbox names are required, independent of the availability of the generic list software mailbox names.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailing list has to have a second address for administration, next to the one people post to. If the list is LIST@DOMAIN, the administration address is LIST-REQUEST@DOMAIN. That address has to exist even when the site runs software that also offers a single mailbox for all of its lists.

sections.title: The DNS Administrator Mailbox
sections.content:
In DNS, the Start of Authority record has a field for the mailbox name of the zone's administrator. That field must be a simple word without metacharacters such as %, ! or ::, and a mail alias should be used on the relevant mail exchanger hosts to direct zone administration mail to the appropriate mailbox.

For simplicity and regularity, the document strongly recommends that the well known mailbox name HOSTMASTER always be used, that is HOSTMASTER@domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Every DNS zone records an administrator. The address stored there has to be plain, with no unusual characters, and the recommendation is to make it the standard hostmaster address so that everyone knows where to write.

sections.title: Autonomous System Mailboxes
sections.content:
Several internet registries run mailing lists for Autonomous System contacts. Mail sent to AS3557@RA.NET would, at the time of writing, reach the technical contact for Autonomous System 3557 in BGP4.

Not all Autonomous Systems are registered with all registries, so an undeliverable mailbox name under this scheme should be treated as an inconvenience rather than as an error or a standards violation.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing registries keep a contact address for each autonomous system, a network or group of networks with its own routing. Writing to that address reaches the right technical contact, though many such addresses simply do not exist, and the document says that is not a fault.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Denial of service attacks, which flood a mailbox with junk, will be easier once this document becomes a standard, since more systems will support the same set of mailbox names.
sections.plainLanguage: Standardising the addresses makes them better known, and that is also the point at which they become easier to flood. The document notes the risk and leaves it there.

viz.caption: The three rules every well known mailbox name must obey

items.title: Top level domain only
items.text: For names that belong to no protocol, only the organisation's top level domain has to be valid. Names for sub-domains may be added.

items.title: Case does not matter
items.text: POSTMASTER, postmaster, Postmaster and PoStMaStEr are the same name and deliver to the same mailbox.

items.title: Acknowledge automatically
items.text: An automatic acknowledgement is usually helpful, with care taken over duelling mail robots and mail loops.
